questions.q: Why is having a quantum error-correcting code not, by itself, sufficient for fault tolerance?
options: A code tells you how to fix an error once it occurs, but doesn't guarantee that the procedures used to fix it won't introduce new errors faster than they can be caught
Codes only work on classical bits, never on real quantum circuits
Fault tolerance only matters for codes with distance less than 3
Error-correcting codes and fault tolerance are exactly the same thing, just different names
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes 'knowing how to correct an error' (the code) from 'guaranteeing the correction process itself doesn't introduce uncontained new errors' (fault tolerance) -- these are genuinely different properties.

questions.q: What does 'fault containment' mean in the precise definition of fault tolerance?
options: Fault containment means no errors can ever occur in a fault-tolerant system
Faults are contained by simply ignoring them during computation
A single physical fault should, at worst, cause a single correctable logical-level error, never an uncontrolled cascade across many qubits
Every fault must be physically isolated in a separate refrigerator unit
questions.explain: Containment is the core requirement: a single faulty gate, ancilla, or measurement should not spread into an error the code can no longer handle.

options: A classical software tool for simulating quantum circuits
A physical piece of specialized refrigeration hardware
Any circuit that uses more than 100 physical qubits
A carefully designed sub-circuit (e.g. for ancilla preparation or syndrome extraction) engineered so a single fault inside it produces at worst one correctable error
questions.explain: Gadgets are the engineered building blocks (ancilla prep, syndrome extraction, specific gates) designed with fault containment as an explicit design goal.

questions.q: Why do transversal gates (previewed in the Steane code lesson) make certain fault-tolerant gadgets easier to build?
options: Transversal gates only exist in classical computing, not quantum computing
Transversal gates always introduce more errors than non-transversal gates
Because a transversal gate acts independently qubit-by-qubit, a single faulty qubit's gate error cannot spread to its neighbors during that operation
Transversal gates eliminate the need for any error correction entirely
questions.explain: Because no qubit's transversal-gate operation touches another qubit, a fault on one qubit during the gate can't propagate to others within that same operation -- directly supporting fault containment.

questions.q: Why must the syndrome-extraction circuitry itself be designed fault-tolerantly, not just the base code?
options: Syndrome-extraction circuits are themselves made of real gates and measurements subject to faults, and a naive design could let a single faulty component spread an error across multiple data qubits during the very process meant to fix errors
Syndrome extraction circuits are purely classical and therefore cannot contain faults
Syndrome extraction is only run once at the very start of a computation, so faults there don't matter
This is not actually necessary; only the logical gates need fault-tolerant design
questions.explain: A careless syndrome-extraction circuit could be self-defeating, letting one faulty gate spread errors during error correction itself -- which is exactly why real fault-tolerant architectures invest heavily in fault-tolerant gadget design for this circuitry specifically.
